tool.name: Go
tool.tagline: Simple, fast compiled language for servers, tools and concurrent systems
tool.description: Go is a statically typed, compiled language from Google with a small spec, fast builds, garbage collection and first-class concurrency via goroutines and channels. It powers cloud infrastructure (Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform), web services and command-line tools. Learn it to build reliable, efficient networked software that is easy to read and deploy as a single binary.

concepts.name: Running code with the go tool
concepts.summary: Install Go, write hello world, and use go run, go build, go fmt and go vet.
concepts.why: Everything in Go — building, testing, formatting, fetching dependencies — goes through one `go` command.
concepts.body:
Go ships as a single toolchain: the compiler, linker, formatter, test runner and dependency manager are all subcommands of `go`. After installing from go.dev/dl, `go version` should print something like `go1.23.4`.

A program lives in a **module**, a directory with a `go.mod` file. Create one with `go mod init example.com/hello`; the path is just a name until you publish it. Put the code from the example in `main.go`, then:

- `go run .` compiles to a temporary binary and runs it — the everyday edit-run loop.
- `go build` produces a real executable named after the module. It is statically linked, so you can copy it to another machine with the same OS/arch and run it. Cross-compile by setting `GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build`.
- `go fmt ./...` (or `gofmt -w .`) rewrites files into the one canonical style. Nobody argues about formatting in Go; editors run it on save.
- `go vet ./...` catches suspicious code the compiler allows, such as a `Printf` verb that doesn't match its argument.
- `go doc fmt.Println` prints documentation from the terminal.

The pattern `./...` means "this directory and every package below it" and works with most subcommands.

Go compiles fast enough that `go run` feels like a scripting language, but you get a native binary with no runtime to install. Note that the compiler is strict: an unused import or unused local variable is a compile error, not a warning — delete it or assign it to `_`.
takeaways: `go mod init <path>` starts a module; `go run .` builds and runs it
`go build` makes a static native binary; set GOOS/GOARCH to cross-compile
`go fmt` and `go vet` are part of the normal workflow
pitfalls: Leaving an unused import or variable — Go refuses to compile it.

quiz.q: You add `import "os"` to main.go but never use it. What happens on `go run .`?
options: Compilation fails with "imported and not used"
It runs and prints a warning
go fmt removes the import automatically before running
quiz.explain: Unused imports (and unused local variables) are compile errors in Go.

concepts.name: Packages, imports and main
concepts.summary: How Go code is split into packages, how imports work, and what makes a program executable.
concepts.why: Every Go file starts with a package clause, and visibility rules depend entirely on package boundaries.
concepts.body:
Every Go file begins with `package name`. All files in one directory form one **package** and share a namespace — a function defined in `a.go` is visible in `b.go` without importing anything.

The package named `main` is special: it builds into an executable, and its `func main()` (no arguments, no return value) is the entry point. Any other package name produces a library that other code imports.

Imports use the package's **import path**: standard library paths are short (`"fmt"`, `"net/http"`), while your own packages are the module path plus the directory, e.g. `"example.com/shop/internal/cart"`. You refer to the imported package by its name — the last path element by convention — so `net/http` is used as `http.Get`.

Visibility is decided by the first letter of an identifier:

- `Total`, `Cart`, `NewCart` start with an upper-case letter and are **exported** — visible to importers.
- `total`, `cart` are unexported — private to the package.

There are no `public`/`private` keywords; capitalisation is the whole rule, and it applies to functions, types, struct fields, methods and constants alike.

A directory named `internal` restricts importers: packages under `a/b/internal/...` can only be imported by code rooted at `a/b`. Use it to keep helpers out of your public API.

Each package may also have `func init()` functions that run automatically before `main`. They are handy for registration but make start-up order implicit, so keep them rare.
takeaways: One directory = one package; `package main` + `func main()` = a program
Upper-case first letter = exported, lower-case = package-private
`internal/` directories limit who may import a package
pitfalls: Trying to call an unexported name like `greet.shout` from another package.

quiz.q: A package `store` declares `type item struct{}` and `func NewItem() *item`. What can another package do?
options: Call `store.NewItem()` and use the result, but not name the type `store.item`
Access all of item's fields regardless of case
quiz.explain: NewItem is exported so it can be called; the type name item is unexported so other packages can't write it, though they can hold the value.

concepts.name: Variables and basic types
concepts.summary: Declare variables with var and :=, meet Go's basic types, zero values and explicit conversions.
concepts.why: Go's static typing, zero values and lack of implicit conversion shape every line you write.
concepts.body:
Go has two ways to declare a variable:

- `var count int` declares with an explicit type; `var name = "Ann"` infers it. `var` works at package level and inside functions.
- `count := 0` is the **short declaration**, inferring the type. It only works inside functions and is what you'll use most of the time.

Every variable starts at its **zero value** — there is no "uninitialized" state. Numbers are `0`, `bool` is `false`, `string` is `""`, and pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions and interfaces are `nil`. Good Go types are designed so the zero value is useful.

The basic types:

- `int`, `int8`…`int64`, `uint`, `uint8`…`uint64`. `int` is 64 bits on all common platforms; use it unless you need a specific size.
- `float64` (prefer it) and `float32`; `complex128`.
- `bool`, `string`, plus aliases `byte` (= `uint8`) and `rune` (= `int32`, a Unicode code point).

Go performs **no implicit conversions**, even between `int` and `int64` or `int` and `float64`. You convert explicitly with `T(x)`: `float64(n) / 2`. Converting a float to an int truncates toward zero.

`:=` needs at least one new variable on its left. In an inner block it creates a *new* variable that shadows the outer one — a classic source of bugs when you meant to assign with `=`.

Use `fmt.Printf("%T %v\n", x, x)` to print a value's type and value while you experiment.
concepts.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var total int // zero value: 0
	price := 2.5  // float64
	qty := 3      // int
	name, ok := "tea", true

	total = int(price * float64(qty)) // explicit conversions
	fmt.Println(total, name, ok)      // 7 tea true

	var s string
	fmt.Printf("%q %T\n", s, qty) // "" int
}
takeaways: `:=` inside functions, `var` when you need the zero value or package scope
Every type has a usable zero value; nothing is uninitialised
No implicit numeric conversions — write `float64(n)`
pitfalls: Accidentally shadowing a variable with `:=` inside an `if` or loop block.

quiz.q: Given `a := 7` and `b := 2.0`, which expression compiles?
quiz.explain: Mixed int/float64 arithmetic needs an explicit conversion; int(b) makes both operands int (float() isn't a Go conversion, and .(T) is only for interfaces).

concepts.name: Constants and iota
concepts.summary: Declare compile-time constants, use untyped constants, and build enumerations with iota.
concepts.why: Constants and iota are how Go expresses fixed values and enum-like sets.
concepts.body:
A **constant** is a value fixed at compile time: `const Pi = 3.14159`. Constants can be numbers, strings, booleans or runes — not slices, maps or structs.

Most constants are **untyped**. `const Big = 1 << 40` has no fixed type; it takes on whatever type the context needs, and arithmetic on untyped constants is done with arbitrary precision. That's why `const Timeout = 5` can be used as an `int` in one place and a `float64` in another, and why `time.Second * 5` works without a conversion. A typed constant, `const Max int32 = 100`, behaves like a value of that type.

Go has no `enum` keyword. Instead, inside a `const ( ... )` block, **iota** starts at 0 and increments on each line. A line with no expression repeats the previous expression with the new iota:

- `KB = 1 << (10 * (iota + 1))` on the first line, then just `MB`, `GB` on the following lines, yields 1024, 1048576, …
- Use `_ = iota` to skip a value, for example to keep the zero value as "unknown".

The idiomatic enum is a named integer type plus constants of that type. Adding a `String() string` method makes values print nicely (the `stringer` tool can generate it). Enums are not closed: any `Weekday(42)` is a legal value, so validate input from outside.
takeaways: Untyped constants adapt to context and are exact at compile time
`iota` counts lines in a const block — Go's enum idiom
Give enum types a String() method for readable output
pitfalls: Assuming Go enums are closed — any integer can be converted to the type.

quiz.q: In `const ( A = iota * 10; B; C )`, what is C?
quiz.explain: B and C repeat the expression `iota * 10` with iota 1 and 2, so C is 20.

concepts.name: if, for and switch
concepts.summary: Go's three control structures: if with an init statement, the single for loop, and switch.
concepts.why: Go deliberately has only one loop and a very regular switch; knowing their forms covers almost all control flow.
concepts.body:
**if** has no parentheses but always needs braces. It can start with a short statement whose variables are scoped to the if/else: `if n, err := strconv.Atoi(s); err == nil { ... }`. This keeps temporary variables out of the surrounding scope and is used constantly with errors.

**for** is Go's only loop, in several shapes:

- `for i := 0; i < 10; i++ { }` — classic three-part loop.
- `for cond { }` — a while loop; `for { }` loops forever.
- `for i, v := range items { }` — iterate slices, arrays, strings, maps and channels. Use `_` to ignore the index.
- `for i := range 10 { }` — since Go 1.22 you can range over an integer: 0 to 9.

Since Go 1.22 each iteration gets a **fresh copy** of the loop variables, so closures and goroutines capturing `i` see the value of that iteration.

`break` and `continue` work as expected; label the outer loop (`outer: for ...` then `break outer`) to exit nested loops.

**switch** compares a value against cases top to bottom and runs the first match. There is **no fall-through** by default — no `break` needed. A case can list several values (`case "sat", "sun":`), and a switch with no expression acts as a clean if/else chain: `switch { case x < 0: ... case x == 0: ... }`. Use the `fallthrough` keyword in the rare case you want to continue into the next case.
takeaways: `for` covers classic, while, infinite and range loops
Use `if x, err := f(); err != nil` to scope temporaries
switch cases don't fall through; list several values per case
pitfalls: Writing `break` inside a switch inside a for loop expecting to leave the loop — it only leaves the switch; use a label.

quiz.q: What does this print? `for i := range 4 { if i == 2 { continue }; fmt.Print(i) }`
quiz.explain: range 4 yields 0..3 and continue skips 2, printing 013.

concepts.name: Functions, multiple returns, closures
concepts.summary: Declare functions, return several values, use variadic parameters, and treat functions as values.
concepts.why: Multiple return values are how Go reports errors, and closures appear in callbacks, sorting and goroutines.
concepts.body:
A function lists parameter names before types: `func add(a, b int) int`. Consecutive parameters of the same type can share it.

Go functions can **return multiple values**. The universal convention is a result plus an error: `func parse(s string) (int, error)`. The caller unpacks both, `n, err := parse(s)`, and uses `_` to discard one it doesn't need. Results can also be **named**, `func split(sum int) (x, y int)`; named results start at their zero values and a bare `return` returns them. Use names for documentation, but avoid bare returns in long functions — they hurt readability.

A **variadic** parameter, `func sum(nums ...int)`, receives a slice. Call it with separate arguments, `sum(1, 2, 3)`, or spread an existing slice with `sum(xs...)`.

Arguments are always passed **by value**: the function gets a copy. (Slices, maps and pointers are small values that *refer* to shared data, which is why modifying a slice's elements is visible to the caller.)

Functions are first-class values. You can store them in variables, pass them as arguments (`sort.Slice(xs, func(i, j int) bool {...})`) and return them. A function literal that refers to variables of the enclosing function is a **closure**: it captures those variables themselves, not copies, so changes are shared and the variables live as long as the closure does.

Go has no default parameter values and no overloading; use distinct names or an options struct instead.
takeaways: Return `(result, error)` and check the error at the call site
Variadic `...T` arrives as a slice; spread a slice with `xs...`
Closures capture variables by reference, not by value
pitfalls: Ignoring a returned error by assigning it to `_` without a good reason.

quiz.q: `c := counter(); c(); c()` then `d := counter(); d()` — what does `d()` return (counter as in the example)?
quiz.explain: Each call to counter creates a new n, so d has its own counter starting from 0 and its first call returns 1.

concepts.name: Arrays and slices
concepts.summary: Fixed-size arrays, the dynamic slices built on them, and how len, cap, append and slicing behave.
concepts.why: Slices are Go's everyday list type; almost every program uses them.
concepts.body:
An **array** has a fixed length that is part of its type: `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types. Arrays are values — assigning or passing one copies every element — so you rarely use them directly.

A **slice**, `[]int`, is a lightweight view onto an underlying array: a pointer, a length and a capacity. You create one with a literal (`[]int{1, 2, 3}`), with `make([]int, len, cap)`, or by slicing an array or slice: `s[low:high]` contains elements `low` up to but not including `high`.

- `len(s)` is the number of elements you can index; `cap(s)` is how far it can grow before reallocating.
- `append(s, x, y)` returns a slice with the elements added. If capacity runs out it allocates a bigger array and copies. **Always assign the result**: `s = append(s, x)`.
- A nil slice (`var s []int`) has length 0 and works fine with `len`, `range` and `append` — no need to initialise it.
- Indexing beyond `len` panics at run time.

Because slicing shares the underlying array, `t := s[1:3]` and `s` see each other's writes. Use `copy(dst, src)` or `slices.Clone(s)` when you need an independent copy.

The standard `slices` package (Go 1.21+) provides the common helpers: `slices.Sort`, `slices.Contains`, `slices.Index`, `slices.Reverse`, `slices.Max`. Reach for it before writing a loop.
takeaways: A slice is a (pointer, len, cap) view onto an array
Always write `s = append(s, ...)`
Sub-slices share memory; clone when you need independence
pitfalls: Calling `append(s, x)` without assigning the result — the new element is lost.

quiz.explain: b views a[1] and a[2]; b[1] is a[2], so a becomes [1 2 9 4].

quiz.q: What is `len(make([]int, 2, 10))`?
quiz.explain: make's second argument is the length; the third is capacity.

concepts.name: Maps
concepts.summary: Create, read, update and delete map entries, test for presence with comma-ok, and iterate.
concepts.why: Maps are Go's built-in hash table, used for lookups, counting, grouping and sets.
concepts.body:
A **map** associates keys with values: `map[string]int`. Keys must be comparable with `==` — strings, numbers, booleans, pointers, channels, and arrays or structs made of those. Slices, maps and functions can't be keys.

Create maps with a literal, `ages := map[string]int{"ann": 31}`, or `make(map[string]int)`. The zero value of a map is `nil`: reading from a nil map is fine (you get zero values), but **writing to a nil map panics**, so always initialise before inserting.

- `m[k] = v` inserts or updates; `delete(m, k)` removes (no-op if absent); `len(m)` counts entries; `clear(m)` empties it.
- `v := m[k]` returns the zero value when the key is missing. To tell "missing" from "present with zero value", use the **comma-ok** form: `v, ok := m[k]`.
- Because missing keys read as zero, counting is just `counts[word]++`.

Iterating with `for k, v := range m` visits entries in a **deliberately randomised order**. If you need a stable order, collect and sort the keys — in Go 1.23+, `slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))` does it in one line.

Maps are reference-like: passing one to a function lets it modify the caller's map. They are **not safe for concurrent writes**; guard them with a mutex if several goroutines modify them. A `map[string]struct{}` (or `map[string]bool`) is the idiomatic set.
takeaways: `v, ok := m[k]` distinguishes missing from zero
Writing to a nil map panics — use `make` or a literal
Map iteration order is random; sort keys for stable output
pitfalls: Writing tests or output that depend on map iteration order.

quiz.q: `var m map[string]int` — which statement panics?
quiz.explain: Reads, len and delete are safe on a nil map; assignment to a nil map panics.

concepts.name: Strings, bytes and runes
concepts.summary: Strings as immutable UTF-8 bytes, runes as code points, and the strings and strconv packages.
concepts.why: Indexing and looping over strings behaves differently from many languages because Go strings are UTF-8 bytes.
concepts.body:
A Go **string** is an immutable sequence of **bytes**, conventionally UTF-8 text. Two consequences matter every day:

- `len(s)` is the number of bytes, not characters. `len("héllo")` is 6 because `é` takes two bytes.
- `s[i]` is a `byte`, and slicing `s[a:b]` slices bytes, which can cut a multi-byte character in half.

A **rune** (alias for `int32`) is a Unicode code point. `for i, r := range s` decodes UTF-8 as it goes, giving the byte offset `i` and the rune `r` — use it whenever you mean "each character". `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)` counts runes, and `[]rune(s)` converts to a slice of runes when you need random access by character.

Strings are immutable, so building one with `+=` in a loop allocates repeatedly. Use `strings.Builder` (or `bytes.Buffer`) to build text efficiently, and convert with `[]byte(s)` / `string(b)` when an API wants bytes (each conversion copies).

The `strings` package covers most text work: `Contains`, `HasPrefix`, `Split`, `Fields`, `Join`, `Replace`, `ToUpper`, `TrimSpace`, `Cut`. Numbers convert with `strconv`: `strconv.Itoa(42)`, `strconv.Atoi("42")`, `strconv.ParseFloat`. Note that `string(65)` gives `"A"` (a rune), not `"65"` — `go vet` warns about it.

Raw string literals in backquotes, like a regex or a multi-line template, ignore escape sequences.
takeaways: Strings are immutable UTF-8 bytes; `len` counts bytes
`range` over a string yields runes; indexing yields bytes
Use strings.Builder for building and strconv for numbers
pitfalls: Using `string(n)` to format an integer — use `strconv.Itoa(n)` or `fmt.Sprint(n)`.

quiz.q: What is the type of `c` in `for _, c := range "go"`?
quiz.explain: Ranging over a string decodes UTF-8 and yields runes (int32).

concepts.name: Structs
concepts.summary: Group fields into struct types, create values with composite literals, and compare and copy them.
concepts.why: Structs are how you model data in Go; there are no classes.
concepts.body:
A **struct** is a typed collection of named fields:

```go
type User struct {
	ID    int
	Name  string
	Admin bool
}
```

Create values with a **composite literal**. Prefer naming the fields, `User{ID: 1, Name: "Ann"}`; omitted fields get their zero values, and the code keeps compiling when fields are added. The positional form `User{1, "Ann", false}` must list every field in order and breaks when the struct changes.

Access fields with a dot: `u.Name`. Field visibility follows the package rule — upper-case fields are exported, which also controls whether packages like `encoding/json` can see them.

Structs are **values**. Assigning `v := u` or passing `u` to a function copies all fields; changing the copy doesn't touch the original. To share and mutate one value, use a pointer (next lesson). Two structs are comparable with `==` when all their fields are comparable, which also makes them usable as map keys.

Anonymous structs, `point := struct{ X, Y int }{1, 2}`, are handy for one-off data such as test tables. The empty struct `struct{}` takes zero bytes and is used for set values and signal-only channels.

A common pattern is a **constructor function** named `NewThing` that validates input and returns a ready-to-use value — Go has no constructors built in, so this is a convention, not a language feature.
takeaways: Use keyed literals: `T{Field: v}`; missing fields are zero
Assignment copies a struct; use pointers to share
Structs with comparable fields support == and can be map keys
pitfalls: Using positional struct literals for types from other packages — they break when fields are added.

quiz.q: `a := Point{1, 2}; b := a; b.X = 9` — what is `a.X`?
quiz.explain: Assigning a struct copies it, so changing b leaves a untouched.

concepts.name: Pointers
concepts.summary: Take addresses with &, dereference with *, and use pointers to share and mutate values.
concepts.why: Pointers decide whether a function sees a copy or the original, and they are central to methods.
concepts.body:
A **pointer** holds the address of a value. `&x` takes the address of `x`, giving a `*int` if x is an `int`; `*p` reads or writes the value it points to. The zero value of a pointer is `nil`, and dereferencing nil panics.

Since Go passes everything by value, a function that must modify its argument takes a pointer:

```go
func reset(n *int) { *n = 0 }
reset(&count)
```

For structs, Go saves you the explicit dereference: if `p` is a `*User`, `p.Name` means `(*p).Name`. `&User{Name: "Ann"}` creates a struct and returns its address in one step, and `new(T)` allocates a zero `T` and returns `*T`.

It is completely safe to return a pointer to a local variable — the compiler notices the value outlives the function and allocates it on the heap. There's no manual memory management; the garbage collector frees values when nothing points to them.

Go has **no pointer arithmetic** (outside the `unsafe` package), which removes a whole class of memory bugs.

When to use a pointer:

- The callee must modify the value.
- The struct is large and copying it on every call would be wasteful.
- You need to represent "no value" with `nil`.

Slices, maps, channels and functions already refer to shared data, so you rarely need a pointer *to* them. For small structs that are not modified, passing by value is simpler and often just as fast.
takeaways: `&x` takes an address, `*p` follows it; zero value is nil
Pass a pointer when the callee must modify the value
Returning a pointer to a local is safe; the GC manages memory
pitfalls: Dereferencing a nil pointer (e.g. a field of a struct you never initialised).

quiz.q: `func f(u User) { u.Name = "x" }` is called as `f(user)`. What happens to `user.Name`?
quiz.explain: f receives a copy of the struct, so the caller's value is not modified.

concepts.name: Slice internals: append and aliasing
concepts.summary: How append grows the backing array, when two slices alias each other, and how to avoid surprises.
concepts.why: Most confusing slice bugs come from not knowing when append reuses memory and when it copies.
concepts.body:
A slice header is three words: a pointer into a backing array, a length and a capacity. Passing a slice copies the header, not the elements, so the callee can change elements the caller sees — but if it appends, the caller's header still has the old length.

`append(s, x)` does one of two things:

- If `len(s) < cap(s)`, it writes `x` into the existing array and returns a header with a longer length. **Any other slice sharing that array sees the write.**
- Otherwise it allocates a new, larger array (roughly doubling for small slices, growing more gently for large ones), copies, and returns a header pointing to the new array. From then on, old and new slices are independent.

That's why this bug is so easy to write: take `a := base[:2]` from a slice of capacity 4, `append(a, 99)` — and you have silently overwritten `base[2]`. Defences:

- Use a **full slice expression** `base[:2:2]` to cap the capacity, forcing the next append to copy.
- Clone with `slices.Clone` before handing a slice to code that may append.
- If a function appends, return the new slice (`s = add(s, x)`) as `append` itself does.

When you know the final size, preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)` to avoid repeated grow-and-copy cycles.

A small sub-slice of a huge array keeps the whole array alive for the garbage collector. When you keep a few bytes of a large buffer, copy them out instead of slicing.
concepts.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	base := make([]int, 4, 4) // [0 0 0 0]
	a := base[:2]             // len 2, cap 4
	a = append(a, 99)         // fits: writes into base[2]
	fmt.Println(base)         // [0 0 99 0]

	b := base[:2:2]   // len 2, cap 2
	b = append(b, 7)  // no room: copies to a new array
	fmt.Println(base) // [0 0 99 0] (unchanged)
	fmt.Println(b)    // [0 0 7]

	out := make([]int, 0, 3) // preallocate capacity
	for i := range 3 {
		out = append(out, i)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(out), cap(out)) // 3 3
}
takeaways: append writes in place while there's capacity, otherwise reallocates
`s[lo:hi:max]` limits capacity so append must copy
Preallocate with `make([]T, 0, n)` when the size is known
pitfalls: Appending to a sub-slice and unknowingly overwriting the parent's elements.

quiz.q: `s := make([]int, 3, 10); t := append(s, 1); u := append(s, 2)` — what is `t[3]`?
quiz.explain: Both appends fit in the same backing array and write index 3; the second write (2) overwrites the first, and t sees it.

concepts.name: Methods and receivers
concepts.summary: Attach methods to your types and choose between value and pointer receivers.
concepts.why: Methods are how Go types get behaviour, and the receiver choice decides which interfaces a type satisfies.
concepts.body:
A **method** is a function with a **receiver** declared before its name:

```go
func (r Rect) Area() float64 { return r.W * r.H }
```

You can define methods on any named type declared in the same package — structs, but also `type Celsius float64` or `type IDs []int`. You can't add methods to types from other packages (wrap them in your own type instead).

The receiver can be a value (`r Rect`) or a pointer (`r *Rect`):

- A **pointer receiver** is required if the method modifies the receiver, and is preferable when the struct is large or contains things that must not be copied, such as a `sync.Mutex`.
- A **value receiver** works on a copy; it suits small, immutable types like `time.Time` or a `Point`.
- Be consistent: if any method needs a pointer receiver, give them all pointer receivers.

Calls are convenient: if `v` is addressable, `v.Scale(2)` automatically becomes `(&v).Scale(2)`, and a pointer automatically dereferences for value methods. The difference shows up with **interfaces**: the method set of `T` contains only value-receiver methods, while `*T` has both. So if `Scale` has a pointer receiver, only `*Rect` — not `Rect` — satisfies an interface that requires `Scale`.

A nil pointer can still call a pointer-receiver method; the method just receives `nil`. Some types use this deliberately, but usually it ends in a nil dereference inside the method.

Method values, `f := r.Area`, bind the receiver and can be passed around like any function.
takeaways: Pointer receivers to mutate or avoid copying; value receivers for small immutable types
Methods can be declared on any named type in your package
Pointer-receiver methods are not in the value type's method set
pitfalls: Mixing value and pointer receivers on one type, then being surprised when T doesn't satisfy an interface.

quiz.q: `func (c Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }` — what does calling `c.Inc()` do to `c.n`?
options: Nothing; the method changes a copy
quiz.explain: A value receiver gets a copy of the struct, so the increment is lost.

concepts.name: Interfaces
concepts.summary: Describe behaviour as a set of methods, satisfied implicitly; type assertions, type switches and any.
concepts.why: Interfaces are Go's main tool for abstraction, testing seams and plugging into the standard library.
concepts.body:
An **interface** type lists method signatures. Any type that has those methods satisfies it **implicitly** — there's no `implements` keyword:

```go
type Shape interface { Area() float64 }
```

Every type with an `Area() float64` method is a `Shape`, including types written before the interface existed. This lets consumers define the small interface they need. The idiom is "accept interfaces, return concrete types", and to keep interfaces small: the standard library's `io.Reader` (`Read(p []byte) (int, error)`), `io.Writer` and `fmt.Stringer` (`String() string`) each have one method, which is why so many types compose with them.

An interface value holds a (dynamic type, dynamic value) pair. `any` (alias for `interface{}`) has no methods, so it can hold anything — use it sparingly, since you lose static checking.

To get the concrete value back:

- **Type assertion**: `s, ok := v.(fmt.Stringer)`. Without `ok`, a failed assertion panics.
- **Type switch**: `switch x := v.(type) { case int: ...; case string: ... }` — `x` has the case's type in each branch.

A frequent gotcha: an interface is `nil` only if both type and value are nil. Returning a nil `*MyErr` as an `error` produces a non-nil interface. Return a literal `nil` instead.

To check at compile time that a type implements an interface, write `var _ Shape = (*Square)(nil)`.
takeaways: Types satisfy interfaces implicitly by having the methods
Keep interfaces small and define them where they are used
Use comma-ok assertions or type switches to recover concrete types
pitfalls: Returning a typed nil pointer as an interface — the interface is not nil.

quiz.q: Which types satisfy `interface{ Close() error }`?
options: Only types that declare they implement it
Only types in the same package as the interface
Any type with a method `Close() error`
quiz.explain: Interface satisfaction is structural and implicit: having the method is enough.

quiz.q: What does `n := v.(int)` do if v holds a string?
quiz.explain: A single-result type assertion panics on mismatch; use `n, ok := v.(int)` to test safely.

concepts.name: Errors and wrapping
concepts.summary: Return errors as values, add context with %w, and inspect them with errors.Is and errors.As.
concepts.why: Explicit error handling is the most visible Go idiom, and good wrapping makes failures debuggable.
concepts.body:
In Go an **error** is just a value implementing `interface { Error() string }`. Functions that can fail return it last, and callers check it immediately:

```go
f, err := os.Open(path)
if err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", err)
}
```

Handle each error once: either deal with it (retry, fallback, log and continue) or return it with added context. Don't log *and* return, or you'll see the same failure several times.

Creating errors:

- `errors.New("msg")` for a fixed message. Exported package-level ones are **sentinel errors**, like `io.EOF` or `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`.
- `fmt.Errorf("parse %q: %w", name, err)` adds context and **wraps** the original. `%v` would only copy the text.
- A custom type (e.g. `type ValidationError struct{ Field string }` with an `Error` method) when callers need structured details.

Inspecting errors — always through the chain of wrapped errors, never by comparing strings:

- `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` reports whether any error in the chain equals the target.
- `errors.As(err, &target)` finds the first error in the chain assignable to `target`'s type and stores it.
- `errors.Join(e1, e2)` combines several errors; `Is`/`As` search all of them.

Error strings are lower-case with no trailing punctuation, since they get prefixed: `open config: read file: permission denied`. Wrapping with `%w` makes the wrapped error part of your API, so wrap deliberately.
takeaways: Return errors as the last result and check them right away
Wrap with `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)`
Use errors.Is for sentinels and errors.As for error types
pitfalls: Comparing `err.Error()` strings or using `==` on wrapped errors instead of errors.Is.

quiz.q: `err := fmt.Errorf("read: %v", io.EOF)` — what does `errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` return?
quiz.explain: %v only formats the text; without %w the original error isn't wrapped, so Is can't find it.

concepts.name: defer, panic and recover
concepts.summary: Schedule cleanup with defer, understand panics, and recover from them at boundaries.
concepts.why: defer is the standard way to release resources, and knowing panic/recover tells you when not to use them.
concepts.body:
A **defer** statement schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns — normally, early, or by panic. Put it right after acquiring a resource so cleanup can't be forgotten:

```go
f, err := os.Open(name)
if err != nil { return err }
defer f.Close()
```

Rules worth knowing:

- Deferred calls run in **last-in, first-out** order.
- The arguments are **evaluated when the defer statement runs**, not when the call happens: `defer fmt.Println(i)` prints the value `i` had at that moment.
- Deferred closures can read and modify **named results**, which is how you can adjust the returned error after the fact.
- defer is per function, not per block. Deferring inside a long loop piles up calls until the function returns — move the loop body into a helper function.

A **panic** stops normal execution, runs the deferred calls up the stack, and crashes the program with a stack trace if nothing stops it. Runtime errors (nil dereference, index out of range) panic, and you can call `panic(v)` yourself — but only for truly unrecoverable programmer errors or impossible states. Expected failures are errors, not panics.

**recover()** called inside a deferred function stops a panic and returns its value; elsewhere it returns nil. Use it at boundaries — an HTTP server recovers per request so one bad handler doesn't kill the process — and convert the panic into an error. A panic in a goroutine can only be recovered inside that goroutine.
takeaways: defer cleanup right after acquiring the resource; runs LIFO
Deferred call arguments are evaluated immediately
panic for bugs, errors for expected failures; recover only in a deferred func
pitfalls: Deferring Close inside a loop over many files — they all stay open until the function returns.

quiz.q: What does this print? `x := 1; defer fmt.Println(x); x = 2`
quiz.explain: The argument x is evaluated when the defer statement executes, when it is still 1.

concepts.name: Modules and go.mod
concepts.summary: Manage dependencies with go.mod and go.sum, go get, go mod tidy, versions and workspaces.
concepts.why: Every real project depends on other modules, and the module system decides what code you actually build.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a tree of packages versioned together, defined by `go.mod` at its root:

```
module example.com/shop

go 1.23

require github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
```

The `module` line is the import path prefix for your packages. The `go` line sets the minimum language version — and since Go 1.21, toolchains will download a newer Go if a module needs it (a `toolchain` line can pin one).

Day-to-day commands:

- `go get example.com/lib@v1.4.0` adds or upgrades a dependency (`@latest` for the newest release).
- `go mod tidy` adds missing requirements and removes unused ones. Run it before committing.
- `go list -m all` shows the full dependency graph; `go mod why -m X` explains why X is needed.

`go.sum` records cryptographic hashes of every module version used; commit it. Downloads go through the module proxy (proxy.golang.org) and are verified against the public checksum database.

Versions follow **semantic versioning**, and Go uses **minimal version selection**: it picks the lowest version satisfying every requirement, so builds are reproducible without a lock file. A breaking change (v2+) must change the import path to `example.com/lib/v2`, so v1 and v2 can coexist.

For local development across modules, `go work init ./app ./lib` creates a `go.work` workspace that builds them together; a `replace` directive in go.mod does the same for one module. Private repositories need `GOPRIVATE=github.com/yourorg/*` so the proxy and checksum database are skipped.
takeaways: go.mod declares the module path, Go version and requirements
`go mod tidy` keeps requirements accurate; commit go.mod and go.sum
Major versions v2+ live at a different import path (`/v2`)
pitfalls: Forgetting to commit go.sum, or editing go.mod by hand instead of using go get / go mod tidy.

quiz.q: Module A needs lib v1.2.0 and module B needs lib v1.4.0. Which version does Go select (v1.5.0 also exists)?
quiz.explain: Minimal version selection picks the lowest version that satisfies all requirements: v1.4.0.

concepts.name: Testing and table-driven tests
concepts.summary: Write tests with the testing package, organise them as tables with subtests, and run them with go test.
concepts.why: Go's built-in testing is used by every project; table tests are the house style.
concepts.body:
Tests live next to the code in files ending `_test.go`. A test is a function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in the same package (or in `pkg_test` for black-box tests). Run them with `go test ./...`; add `-v` for verbose output, `-run 'Parse/negative'` to filter, `-cover` for coverage, and `-count=1` to bypass the result cache.

`*testing.T` reports failures:

- `t.Errorf(...)` records a failure and keeps going — preferred, so one run shows all problems.
- `t.Fatalf(...)` stops this test immediately — use it when continuing makes no sense.
- `t.Helper()` in helper functions makes failures point to the caller's line.
- `t.Cleanup(fn)`, `t.TempDir()` and `t.Setenv()` handle setup and teardown.

The idiomatic shape is a **table-driven test**: a slice of cases, each with a name, inputs and expected output, looped over with `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`. Each case becomes a **subtest** that can be run alone and reports separately. Adding a case is one line, which encourages covering edge cases.

Go's style is plain comparisons and clear messages — `got X, want Y` — rather than assertion libraries. For deep comparisons use `reflect.DeepEqual`, `slices.Equal`, or a diff library such as go-cmp.

Calling `t.Parallel()` lets subtests run concurrently. Example functions (`func ExampleAdd()` with an `// Output:` comment) are compiled, run, and shown in the docs, and `go test -fuzz` adds native fuzzing.
takeaways: Tests are `TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in `_test.go` files; run `go test ./...`
Table-driven tests + `t.Run` subtests are the idiomatic structure
Prefer t.Errorf to keep going; t.Fatalf when you can't continue
pitfalls: Using t.Fatal from a goroutine other than the test's own — it must be called from the test goroutine.

quiz.q: How do you run only the "negative" case of TestAbs?
quiz.explain: -run takes a regex per level of test/subtest name separated by slashes.

concepts.name: Goroutines
concepts.summary: Start concurrent work with the go keyword and understand what goroutines are and cost.
concepts.why: Goroutines are the foundation of every concurrent Go program, from servers to pipelines.
concepts.body:
A **goroutine** is a function running concurrently with the rest of the program. You start one by putting `go` before a call: `go handle(conn)`. The call returns immediately; the function runs independently.

Goroutines are cheap. Each starts with a small stack (a few kilobytes) that grows as needed, and the Go runtime multiplexes them onto a handful of OS threads. Running thousands — even hundreds of thousands — is normal. A web server typically uses one goroutine per request.

Things to keep in mind:

- When `main` returns, the program exits, **killing any goroutines still running**. You must explicitly wait for work you care about, using channels or `sync.WaitGroup` (coming next).
- `go` discards the function's return values. Results come back through channels or shared, synchronised variables.
- Goroutines share memory. If two of them access the same variable and at least one writes, you need synchronisation, or you have a **data race**.
- Since Go 1.22, loop variables are per-iteration, so `for _, url := range urls { go fetch(url) }` and closures capturing `url` are safe. In older code you'll see `url := url` copies for this reason.

Every goroutine you start should have a clear way to finish. A goroutine blocked forever on a channel nobody will send to is a **goroutine leak**: it holds its memory until the process exits. Think about who stops each goroutine before you write `go`.

`time.Sleep` to "wait for goroutines" only appears in toy examples; real code synchronises.
takeaways: `go f()` starts f concurrently and returns immediately
Goroutines are cheap, but the program exits when main returns
Every goroutine needs a defined way to finish
pitfalls: Starting goroutines in main and returning before they finish, so their work silently never happens.

quiz.q: main starts `go fmt.Println("hi")` and then returns immediately. What is printed?
options: Possibly nothing — main may exit before the goroutine runs
quiz.explain: Program exit doesn't wait for other goroutines, so the print may never happen.

concepts.name: Channels
concepts.summary: Send and receive values between goroutines with unbuffered and buffered channels, close and range.
concepts.why: Channels are Go's primary way for goroutines to communicate and synchronise.
concepts.body:
A **channel** is a typed conduit between goroutines: `ch := make(chan int)`. `ch <- v` sends, `v := <-ch` receives. Go's motto: *share memory by communicating*.

An **unbuffered** channel synchronises: a send blocks until a receiver takes the value, so it doubles as a handshake. A **buffered** channel, `make(chan int, 10)`, lets sends proceed until the buffer is full and receives proceed while it has values. Buffers smooth out bursts; they don't fix a design where nobody receives.

**Closing**: `close(ch)` tells receivers no more values are coming. After close, receives drain any buffered values and then return the zero value immediately; `v, ok := <-ch` gives `ok == false` once closed and empty. `for v := range ch` loops until the channel is closed and drained — the standard consumer loop. Rules:

- Only the **sender** closes, and only when receivers need to know it's done. Not every channel needs closing.
- Sending on a closed channel panics; closing twice panics.
- A nil channel blocks forever on both send and receive.

Directional types document intent and are enforced by the compiler: `chan<- int` is send-only, `<-chan int` receive-only. Functions that produce values typically return `<-chan T`.

If every goroutine is blocked on channel operations, the runtime aborts with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` — the most common first channel bug, usually a send nobody receives.
takeaways: Unbuffered channels hand off and synchronise; buffered ones queue
The sender closes; receivers use `range` or `v, ok := <-ch`
Use directional types `<-chan T` / `chan<- T` in signatures
pitfalls: Closing a channel from the receiver side or from several senders — causes send-on-closed panics.

quiz.q: What happens when you receive from a closed, empty `chan int`?
options: It returns the last value sent
quiz.explain: Receives on a closed channel never block; once drained they return the zero value with ok == false.

concepts.name: select and timeouts
concepts.summary: Wait on several channel operations at once, add timeouts, and do non-blocking sends and receives.
concepts.why: select is how goroutines react to whichever event comes first: data, cancellation or a deadline.
concepts.body:
A **select** statement waits on several channel operations and runs the case for whichever is ready first:

```go
select {
case msg := <-inbox:
	handle(msg)
case out <- next:
	sent++
case <-quit:
	return
}
```

If several cases are ready at once, select picks one **at random**, so no channel can starve the others. If none is ready, it blocks.

Common patterns:

- **Timeouts**: add `case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):` to give up waiting. In a long-running loop, prefer one `time.NewTimer` or a context deadline, because each `time.After` call creates a new timer.
- **Non-blocking operations**: a `default` case runs immediately when nothing else is ready. `select { case ch <- v: default: dropped++ }` sends if possible and drops otherwise.
- **Cancellation**: include `case <-ctx.Done():` (next lessons) so a goroutine stops when its work is no longer wanted.
- **Event loops**: `for { select { ... } }` is the standard shape for a goroutine that serves several channels.

A nil channel is never ready, which is a useful trick: set a channel variable to `nil` to disable its case once it's closed, while still serving the others.

An empty `select {}` blocks forever. And a `default` case inside a `for` loop turns it into a busy loop that burns CPU — only use `default` when you genuinely have something else to do.
takeaways: select runs the first ready case; ties are broken randomly
`time.After` or a context gives you timeouts
`default` makes an operation non-blocking — avoid it in tight loops
pitfalls: Using an unbuffered result channel with a timeout: when the timeout wins, the sender blocks forever and leaks.

quiz.q: In the example, why is slowQuery's channel buffered with capacity 1?
options: So the goroutine can send and exit even if nobody receives after the timeout
quiz.explain: If the caller stopped waiting, an unbuffered send would block forever and leak the goroutine.

concepts.name: sync.WaitGroup and Mutex
concepts.summary: Wait for a group of goroutines, protect shared state with Mutex and RWMutex, and run setup once.
concepts.why: Not everything fits channels; WaitGroup and Mutex are the simplest correct tools for many jobs.
concepts.body:
**sync.WaitGroup** waits for a set of goroutines to finish:

- `wg.Add(n)` before starting the goroutines (in the launching goroutine, not inside the new one).
- `defer wg.Done()` at the top of each goroutine.
- `wg.Wait()` blocks until the counter reaches zero.

(Go 1.25 adds `wg.Go(f)`, which does the Add/Done bookkeeping for you.)

**sync.Mutex** gives mutual exclusion around shared state: `mu.Lock()`, then `defer mu.Unlock()`. Embed the mutex next to the data it protects, in the same struct, and keep critical sections short — never hold a lock while doing I/O or waiting on a channel. **sync.RWMutex** allows many concurrent readers (`RLock`) or one writer (`Lock`); it only pays off when reads greatly outnumber writes.

Other useful pieces:

- `sync.Once` (or `sync.OnceValue`, Go 1.21+) runs initialisation exactly once, even with concurrent callers.
- `sync/atomic` types such as `atomic.Int64` for simple counters and flags.
- `sync.Map` for specialised caches; a plain map plus a mutex is usually clearer.

A mutex or WaitGroup **must not be copied** after first use. Pass structs containing them by pointer and use pointer receivers; `go vet` flags copies.

When should you use a mutex instead of a channel? Use channels to pass ownership of data or coordinate stages of work; use a mutex when goroutines simply need safe access to a shared structure such as a cache or counter.
takeaways: WaitGroup: Add before `go`, `defer Done()` inside, Wait to join
Keep the Mutex next to the data it guards; lock briefly
Never copy a Mutex or WaitGroup — use pointers
pitfalls: Calling wg.Add(1) inside the goroutine, racing with wg.Wait().

quiz.q: Why is `Record` declared with a pointer receiver?
options: A value receiver would lock a copy of the mutex, so nothing would be protected
Maps can't be used with value receivers
quiz.explain: With a value receiver each call copies the struct, including its Mutex, so the lock guards nothing shared.

concepts.name: context: cancellation and deadlines
concepts.summary: Propagate cancellation, timeouts and request-scoped values through call chains with context.Context.
concepts.why: Every server, client and long-running operation in Go is expected to accept a context and stop when it's done.
concepts.body:
A **context.Context** carries a cancellation signal, an optional deadline and request-scoped values down a call chain. By convention it is the **first parameter**, named `ctx`: `func Fetch(ctx context.Context, url string) error`.

Contexts form a tree. Start from `context.Background()` (in main, tests, top-level) and derive children:

- `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)` — cancelled when you call `cancel()`.
- `context.WithTimeout(parent, 2*time.Second)` / `WithDeadline` — cancelled automatically at the deadline.
- Cancelling a parent cancels all its children.

**Always `defer cancel()`** right after creating a derived context; it releases the timer and resources even when the work finishes early. `go vet` warns if you forget.

Code doing the work checks for cancellation:

- `<-ctx.Done()` is a channel that closes on cancellation — use it in a `select`.
- `ctx.Err()` then returns `context.Canceled` or `context.DeadlineExceeded`.
- Pass `ctx` on to everything that blocks: `http.NewRequestWithContext`, database queries, your own functions.

`context.WithValue` attaches request-scoped data such as a trace ID, using an unexported key type to avoid collisions. Don't use it to pass optional function parameters.

Don't store contexts in structs; pass them explicitly. Use `context.TODO()` as a placeholder when you haven't plumbed one through yet. Go 1.21 added `context.WithoutCancel` and `context.AfterFunc` for advanced cases.
takeaways: Pass `ctx context.Context` as the first parameter, never store it
Derive with WithCancel/WithTimeout and always `defer cancel()`
Blocking code selects on `ctx.Done()` and returns `ctx.Err()`
pitfalls: Ignoring ctx inside a loop or blocking call, so cancellation never actually stops the work.

quiz.q: A parent context is cancelled. What happens to a child created with context.WithTimeout(parent, time.Hour)?
options: It keeps running until its hour is up
quiz.explain: Cancellation propagates from parent to all derived children, regardless of their own deadlines.

concepts.name: JSON and struct tags
concepts.summary: Encode and decode JSON with encoding/json, control field names with struct tags, and stream data.
concepts.why: JSON is the lingua franca of APIs and config, and struct tags are how Go maps it to types.
concepts.body:
The `encoding/json` package converts between Go values and JSON:

- `json.Marshal(v)` returns `[]byte`; `json.MarshalIndent` pretty-prints.
- `json.Unmarshal(data, &v)` decodes into a pointer.
- `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)` and `json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&v)` stream to and from an `io.Writer` / `io.Reader`, such as an HTTP body.

Only **exported** fields are encoded; lower-case fields are silently ignored — the classic "my JSON is `{}`" bug. **Struct tags** customise the mapping:

```go
type User struct {
	ID       int    `json:"id"`
	Email    string `json:"email,omitempty"`
	Password string `json:"-"`
}
```

- `json:"name"` sets the key; `-` skips the field.
- `omitempty` drops zero values (empty string, 0, nil, empty slice or map). It doesn't treat an empty struct as empty. Newer Go versions (1.24+) add `omitzero` for that.
- Matching on decode is case-insensitive, and unknown keys are ignored unless you call `dec.DisallowUnknownFields()`.

Type mapping: objects decode into structs or `map[string]any`, arrays into slices, numbers into any numeric field — and into `float64` when the target is `any`. Use a pointer field (`*int`) when you must distinguish "missing" from zero. `time.Time` encodes as RFC 3339.

For custom formats, implement `MarshalJSON`/`UnmarshalJSON`, or `encoding.TextMarshaler` for values that are naturally strings. `json.RawMessage` defers decoding of part of a document.
takeaways: Only exported fields are (un)marshalled
Struct tags set names: `json:"name,omitempty"`, `json:"-"`
Use Decoder/Encoder for streams like HTTP bodies
pitfalls: Passing a value instead of a pointer to json.Unmarshal — it returns an InvalidUnmarshalError.

quiz.q: A struct has field `count int` with tag `json:"count"`. What does Marshal output for it?
options: Nothing; the field is unexported so it's skipped
quiz.explain: encoding/json ignores unexported fields even if they have a tag.

concepts.name: HTTP servers and clients
concepts.summary: Build an HTTP API with net/http's ServeMux routing patterns and call services with a configured client.
concepts.why: net/http is production-grade; many Go services use nothing else for HTTP.
concepts.body:
`net/http` contains both a production-ready server and a client.

**Server.** A handler is anything implementing `ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`; usually you register functions on a `*http.ServeMux`. Since Go 1.22 patterns include the method and wildcards:

- `mux.HandleFunc("GET /items/{id}", getItem)` — read the wildcard with `r.PathValue("id")`.
- `"POST /items"` matches only POST; a mismatched method gets a 405 automatically.
- `"/static/"` with a trailing slash matches the whole subtree; `{path...}` captures the rest.

In a handler, set headers with `w.Header().Set(...)` **before** `w.WriteHeader(status)` or the first `Write`. `r.Context()` is cancelled when the client disconnects. Each request runs in its own goroutine, so shared state needs synchronisation.

**Middleware** is just a function `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` wrapping another handler — for logging, auth or recovering panics.

Use an explicit `http.Server` with timeouts rather than `http.ListenAndServe`, which has none; slow clients could otherwise hold connections forever. For graceful shutdown, call `srv.Shutdown(ctx)` on SIGTERM.

**Client.** `http.Get` uses `http.DefaultClient`, which has **no timeout**. Create a client with `&http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}` and reuse it — it pools connections. Build requests with `http.NewRequestWithContext`, always `defer resp.Body.Close()`, and check `resp.StatusCode`: a 404 or 500 is not an error.

`net/http/httptest` lets you test handlers without a network (`httptest.NewRecorder`) or spin up a real test server.
takeaways: Go 1.22+ ServeMux patterns: `"GET /items/{id}"` + `r.PathValue`
Set server and client timeouts; the defaults have none
Always close resp.Body and check StatusCode yourself
pitfalls: Calling w.Header().Set after w.WriteHeader or Write — the header is already sent and the change is ignored.

quiz.q: `resp, err := client.Get(url)` returns a 500 response. What is err?
options: nil — HTTP error statuses are not Go errors
quiz.explain: The client returns an error only for transport failures; you must check resp.StatusCode.

concepts.name: Embedding and composition
concepts.summary: Compose types by embedding structs and interfaces, and understand method promotion and its limits.
concepts.why: Go has no inheritance; embedding is how you reuse behaviour and build bigger interfaces from small ones.
concepts.body:
A struct can **embed** another type by listing it without a field name:

```go
type Logger struct{ prefix string }
func (l *Logger) Log(msg string) { fmt.Println(l.prefix + msg) }

type Service struct {
	*Logger
	name string
}
```

The embedded type's fields and methods are **promoted**: `svc.Log("hi")` works as if `Service` declared `Log`, and `Service` now satisfies any interface that `Log` helps satisfy. The embedded value is still a normal field, named after its type: `svc.Logger`.

This is **composition, not inheritance**:

- Promoted methods run with the embedded value as receiver. Inside `Log`, `l` is the `*Logger`, and it knows nothing about the outer `Service`. There's no virtual dispatch back to the outer type.
- An outer method or field with the same name **shadows** the promoted one; you can still call `svc.Logger.Log` explicitly.
- If two embedded types at the same depth provide the same name, using that name is a compile error (ambiguous selector) — but only when you actually use it.

**Interfaces embed interfaces** to build larger contracts: `io.ReadWriter` is `interface{ Reader; Writer }`.

Embedding an **interface in a struct** is a useful trick for wrapping: the struct satisfies the whole interface, and you override only the methods you care about. It's common in tests and decorators, but calling a non-overridden method on a nil embedded interface panics.

Be careful embedding types in exported structs: every promoted method becomes part of your public API — including embedding `sync.Mutex`, which exports `Lock` and `Unlock`.
takeaways: Embedded fields' methods are promoted to the outer type
Promoted methods see only the inner value — no virtual dispatch
Embed interfaces to compose contracts or to wrap and override
pitfalls: Embedding a type in an exported struct and accidentally exposing its methods (e.g. Lock/Unlock) as API.

quiz.q: Service embeds *Logger whose Log method calls l.Prefix(). Service also defines its own Prefix(). Which Prefix runs when you call svc.Log()?
quiz.explain: Inside Log the receiver is the *Logger, so it calls Logger.Prefix; Go has no overriding through embedding.

concepts.name: Generics: type parameters
concepts.summary: Write functions and types with type parameters, use constraints like comparable and cmp.Ordered.
concepts.why: Generics remove copy-paste and any-casting from containers and algorithms while staying type-safe.
concepts.body:
Since Go 1.18, functions and types can take **type parameters** in square brackets:

```go
func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U
```

Each type parameter has a **constraint** — an interface describing what the type must support:

- `any` — no requirements; you can only move and store values.
- `comparable` — supports `==` and `!=`, required for map keys.
- `cmp.Ordered` — supports `<`, `>`; covers integers, floats and strings.
- Your own: `type Number interface { ~int | ~int64 | ~float64 }`. A **type set** like this lists permitted types; `~int` means "any type whose underlying type is int", so a `type Celsius int` qualifies too. Constraints can also require methods.

Callers rarely write type arguments: in `Map(nums, strconv.Itoa)` the compiler **infers** `T` and `U`. You need explicit arguments only when inference has nothing to go on, such as `Zero[int]()`.

Generic types work the same way: `type Stack[T any] struct{ items []T }`, with methods `func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T)`. Methods cannot introduce *new* type parameters of their own — write a top-level function instead.

When to use them: containers, and algorithms over slices, maps and channels (the `slices` and `maps` packages are generic). When not to: if an ordinary interface with methods expresses the behaviour, prefer it. A good rule is to write the concrete code first and introduce type parameters when you find yourself duplicating it for several types.

Inside generic code you can't use a type switch on `T` directly; you'd convert to `any` first, which is a sign generics may be the wrong tool.
takeaways: Type parameters go in brackets with a constraint: `[T cmp.Ordered]`
`~T` in a constraint admits types with underlying type T
Type arguments are usually inferred from the call
pitfalls: Reaching for generics where a plain interface with methods is simpler and clearer.

quiz.q: `type Celsius float64`. Which constraint lets `Sum[Celsius]` compile?
quiz.explain: `~float64` includes every type whose underlying type is float64; plain `float64` admits only float64 itself.

concepts.name: Range-over-func iterators
concepts.summary: Write and consume Go 1.23 iterators: iter.Seq, iter.Seq2, yield, and the iterator helpers in slices and maps.
concepts.why: Iterators give custom collections and lazy sequences the same `for range` syntax as slices and maps.
concepts.body:
Go 1.23 lets `for range` loop over **functions**. An iterator is a function that takes a `yield` callback and calls it once per element:

```go
func(yield func(V) bool)       // iter.Seq[V]
func(yield func(K, V) bool)    // iter.Seq2[K, V]
```

The `iter` package names these types. When you write `for v := range seq { ... }`, the compiler turns the loop body into the `yield` function. `yield` returns `false` when the loop stops early (via `break`, `return` or a panic), and the iterator **must** stop calling it then — calling yield after it returned false panics at run time. The standard shape is:

```go
if !yield(v) { return }
```

These are **push iterators**: the sequence drives the loop. `iter.Pull` converts one into a pull-style `next()`/`stop()` pair when you need to step through two sequences in lockstep; always call `stop` when done.

The standard library embraces them:

- `slices.All`, `slices.Values`, `slices.Backward`, `slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted`.
- `maps.Keys`, `maps.Values`, `maps.All`, `maps.Collect`.
- Go 1.24 added `strings.Lines`, `strings.SplitSeq` and friends.

Iterators are **lazy**: nothing is computed until the loop asks, so infinite sequences and pipelines that stop early are cheap. Their natural partner is generics: functions like `Filter[V any](seq iter.Seq[V], keep func(V) bool) iter.Seq[V]` compose cleanly.

A method that returns an iterator is conventionally named `All`, or after what it yields (`Keys`, `Lines`). Most iterators can be ranged over more than once; document it if yours can't.
takeaways: `iter.Seq[V]` is `func(yield func(V) bool)`; range over it directly
Stop as soon as yield returns false
slices and maps provide All/Values/Keys/Collect/Sorted helpers
pitfalls: Ignoring yield's return value — breaking out of the loop then causes a runtime panic.

quiz.q: A consumer `break`s out of `for v := range seq`. What does seq's yield call return at that point?
quiz.explain: yield returns false when the loop body stops early; the iterator must then return without calling yield again.

concepts.name: Concurrency patterns: pipelines and fan-out
concepts.summary: Compose goroutines and channels into pipelines, fan-out/fan-in, and cancellable stages with errgroup.
concepts.why: Real concurrent programs are built from a few well-known patterns that also guarantee goroutines exit.
concepts.body:
A **pipeline** is a series of stages connected by channels. Each stage is a function that receives values from an input channel, processes them, and sends to an output channel it owns and closes:

```go
func square(ctx context.Context, in <-chan int) <-chan int
```

Two rules keep pipelines correct:

- **The stage that creates a channel closes it**, with `defer close(out)` in its goroutine, so downstream `range` loops end.
- **Every send also selects on `ctx.Done()`**. If the consumer quits early, upstream goroutines must be able to give up instead of blocking forever on a send — otherwise they leak.

**Fan-out** means starting several goroutines reading from the same input channel to parallelise a slow stage; Go distributes values between them. **Fan-in** (merge) combines several channels into one: start a goroutine per input that forwards values, and a final goroutine that waits on a WaitGroup and closes the output.

For the very common "run N tasks concurrently, stop on first error" case, use `golang.org/x/sync/errgroup`:

- `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`; `g.Go(func() error {...})` for each task.
- The first error cancels `ctx`, so sibling tasks can stop early; `g.Wait()` returns that error.
- `g.SetLimit(n)` bounds concurrency.

A **semaphore** — a buffered channel of capacity n where you send to acquire and receive to release — is the simplest way to cap parallelism by hand.

Ordering is lost once you fan out. If results must stay in input order, carry an index with each item and reassemble, or write results into a preallocated slice at that index.
takeaways: Each stage owns and closes its output channel
Every blocking send also selects on ctx.Done() to prevent leaks
errgroup covers run-N-tasks-and-stop-on-first-error
pitfalls: A consumer that stops reading early without cancelling, leaving upstream goroutines blocked forever.

quiz.q: In a fan-in merge of three input channels, when is it safe to close the output channel?
options: Right after starting the forwarding goroutines
Never; output channels must not be closed
After all forwarding goroutines have finished (WaitGroup.Wait)
quiz.explain: Closing earlier would make a still-running forwarder send on a closed channel and panic.

concepts.name: Worker pools and rate limiting
concepts.summary: Bound concurrency with a fixed pool of workers reading a job channel, collect results and errors, and pace work.
concepts.why: Unbounded goroutines can exhaust memory, file descriptors or a downstream service; pools keep load predictable.
concepts.body:
Starting one goroutine per item is fine for a hundred items, but not for a million URLs or rows, and it can overwhelm whatever you're calling. A **worker pool** fixes concurrency at N:

1. Create a `jobs` channel and a `results` channel.
2. Start N worker goroutines, each running `for j := range jobs { results <- process(j) }`.
3. Feed jobs from another goroutine and `close(jobs)` when done — this is what ends the workers' loops.
4. When all workers have returned (a WaitGroup), close `results` so the collector's `range` ends.

Choose N based on the bottleneck: around `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)` for CPU-bound work; for I/O-bound work, the limit the remote system tolerates (often tens).

Carry errors in the result type (`type result struct { id int; err error }`) rather than dropping them, and decide whether one failure should cancel the rest — if so, use a context or `errgroup` with `SetLimit(n)`, which is effectively a worker pool with error handling built in.

To limit **rate** rather than concurrency, use a `time.Ticker` to pace job submission, or the token-bucket `golang.org/x/time/rate.Limiter` whose `Wait(ctx)` blocks until a request is allowed.

Size channel buffers deliberately. A buffered `jobs` channel lets the producer run ahead; an unbuffered one gives natural back-pressure. Large buffers mostly hide problems.

Remember results arrive in completion order, not submission order; include an id if the caller needs to match them up.
takeaways: N workers ranging over a jobs channel bound concurrency to N
Close jobs to stop workers; close results after wg.Wait()
Use rate.Limiter or a Ticker when the limit is requests per second
pitfalls: Closing the results channel from a worker, or before all workers finish — causes a send-on-closed panic.

quiz.q: In the example, what would happen if `close(jobs)` were removed?
options: Workers exit after the last job anyway
Workers block forever, wg.Wait never returns, and main deadlocks
Results are lost but the program exits
quiz.explain: Workers' range loops only end when jobs is closed; without it results is never closed and main's range blocks.

concepts.name: Data races and the race detector
concepts.summary: What a data race is, why it's undefined behaviour in practice, and how go test -race finds them.
concepts.why: Races cause rare, unreproducible bugs in production; the race detector catches most of them in testing.
concepts.body:
A **data race** happens when two goroutines access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and nothing orders them (no mutex, channel or atomic). Races are not just "lost updates": the compiler and CPU may reorder or cache operations, and a race on a multi-word value — a string, slice, interface or map — can produce torn values and crashes. Concurrent map writes even trigger a fatal runtime error.

Go ships a **race detector**. Enable it with the `-race` flag:

- `go test -race ./...` — the most valuable place; run it in CI.
- `go run -race .` or `go build -race` for manual testing of a binary.

It instruments memory accesses and reports races that **actually happen during the run**, with stack traces for both accesses and where the goroutines were created. It has no false positives, but it can only find races your tests exercise — so tests should run the concurrent code paths. Expect roughly 5–10× slower execution and more memory; it's for testing, not production builds. It requires cgo on most platforms.

Fixing a race means establishing **happens-before** ordering:

- Protect the data with a `sync.Mutex`.
- Use `sync/atomic` types for single counters or flags.
- Transfer ownership through a channel so only one goroutine touches the data at a time.
- Give each goroutine its own data, such as its own slice index, and combine after `wg.Wait()`.

"It's only a counter, the occasional wrong value is fine" is not a valid excuse — racy programs have no guaranteed behaviour at all.
takeaways: A race = concurrent access, one write, no synchronisation
`go test -race ./...` in CI; it finds races that occur during the run
Fix with mutexes, atomics, channels or not sharing at all
pitfalls: Assuming no race report means no races — the detector only sees code paths that ran concurrently.

quiz.q: The race detector reports nothing for your test suite. What can you conclude?
options: No races occurred in the executions the tests performed
Only that there are no map races
quiz.explain: It detects races dynamically, so code paths not exercised concurrently by the tests may still race.

concepts.name: Benchmarks and pprof profiling
concepts.summary: Measure performance with testing benchmarks and benchstat, then find hot spots with CPU and heap profiles.
concepts.why: Optimising without measuring wastes time; Go's built-in benchmarks and pprof make measuring easy.
concepts.body:
A **benchmark** is a function `func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` in a `_test.go` file. Run the code under test `b.N` times; the framework increases `b.N` until timing is stable:

```go
for range b.N { Parse(input) }
```

(Go 1.24 adds `for b.Loop() { ... }`, which also prevents the compiler from optimising the work away and excludes setup automatically.)

Run with `go test -bench=. -benchmem`. Output shows ns/op, and with `-benchmem` also B/op and allocs/op — allocations are often the real cost. Use `b.ReportAllocs()`, `b.ResetTimer()` after expensive setup, and sub-benchmarks with `b.Run` to compare sizes. Results are noisy: run with `-count=10` before and after a change and compare with **benchstat** (`golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat`), which tells you whether a difference is statistically significant.

To find *where* time goes, profile:

- `go test -bench=Parse -cpuprofile cpu.out -memprofile mem.out`
- `go tool pprof -http=:8081 cpu.out` opens a web UI with flame graphs, top functions and annotated source.
- In a running service, `import _ "net/http/pprof"` registers `/debug/pprof/` handlers. Then `go tool pprof http://host:port/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30` grabs a CPU profile; `/heap`, `/goroutine`, `/mutex` and `/block` show other views. Don't expose these endpoints publicly.

`go tool trace` shows scheduler, GC and goroutine timelines when profiles aren't enough. And **profile-guided optimisation**: put a representative CPU profile at `default.pgo` in the main package and `go build` uses it to inline and devirtualise hot paths, typically gaining a few percent.
takeaways: `BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B)` + `go test -bench=. -benchmem`
Compare runs with benchstat, not by eyeballing one result
pprof (files or net/http/pprof) shows where CPU and memory go
pitfalls: Benchmarking code whose result is unused, letting the compiler eliminate the work you meant to measure.

quiz.q: Which flag adds allocation statistics (B/op, allocs/op) to benchmark output?
quiz.explain: -benchmem reports memory allocation stats for every benchmark.

concepts.name: Reflection with reflect
concepts.summary: Inspect types and values at run time with reflect.TypeOf and ValueOf, read struct tags, and set fields.
concepts.why: Reflection powers encoding/json, ORMs and validators; you need it to write such libraries and to understand them.
concepts.body:
The `reflect` package lets a program examine values whose type isn't known at compile time. It starts from an interface value:

- `reflect.TypeOf(x)` returns a `reflect.Type`: its `Name()`, `Kind()` (Struct, Slice, Ptr, Int…), and for structs `NumField()` and `Field(i)`, which includes the field's name and **tag** (`f.Tag.Get("json")`).
- `reflect.ValueOf(x)` returns a `reflect.Value` holding the data, with accessors like `Int()`, `String()`, `Len()`, `Index(i)`, `Field(i)`, `MapRange()`.

**Kind vs Type**: a `type UserID int` has Type `UserID` but Kind `Int`. Generic reflection code switches on Kind.

To **modify** a value through reflection you need an addressable value: pass a pointer and call `Elem()`, as in `reflect.ValueOf(&cfg).Elem()`. `v.CanSet()` reports whether setting is allowed; unexported fields are readable but not settable. Calling `SetInt` on a non-settable value, or `Int()` on a non-integer Kind, **panics** — reflection trades compile-time checks for run-time panics.

The Laws of Reflection summarise it: reflection goes from interface value to reflection object and back (`v.Interface()`), and to modify a reflection object the value must be settable.

Costs: reflective code is slower (often 10–100× for field access), allocates, and is harder to read. Prefer interfaces, generics or code generation (`go generate`) when they fit, and keep reflection at the edges — serialisation, dependency injection, test helpers. Cache per-type information such as parsed tags, since inspecting a Type repeatedly is wasteful.
takeaways: TypeOf for type info (Kind, fields, tags), ValueOf for data
To set via reflection, start from a pointer and call Elem()
Reflection errors are run-time panics; keep it at the edges
pitfalls: Calling reflect.ValueOf(cfg) (not &cfg) and then trying to set a field — it panics because the value isn't addressable.

quiz.q: `type Celsius float64; var c Celsius` — what is `reflect.TypeOf(c).Kind()`?
quiz.explain: Kind is the underlying category of the type; the named type Celsius has Kind Float64.

concepts.name: The scheduler: G, M and P
concepts.summary: How the Go runtime multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads: run queues, work stealing, syscalls, preemption.
concepts.why: Understanding the scheduler explains goroutine costs, GOMAXPROCS tuning, and odd latency or CPU behaviour.
concepts.body:
The runtime scheduler juggles three kinds of objects:

- **G** — a goroutine: its stack, instruction pointer and status.
- **M** — a machine, i.e. an OS thread that executes code.
- **P** — a processor: the right to run Go code, plus a local run queue of runnable Gs. There are exactly `GOMAXPROCS` Ps.

An M must hold a P to run Go code, so `GOMAXPROCS` caps how many goroutines execute Go code simultaneously. It defaults to the number of CPUs; since Go 1.25 it also respects a container's cgroup CPU limit, which older versions ignored (hence the popular `automaxprocs` package).

Scheduling flow: `go f()` puts the new G in the current P's local queue (in a `runnext` slot, so it tends to run soon). When a P's queue empties it checks the global queue, the network poller, and then **steals half** of another P's queue. This keeps all cores busy without a central lock.

Blocking is handled differently by cause:

- Channel, mutex or sleep: the G is parked and the M simply runs another G — cheap.
- Network I/O: the G parks on the **netpoller** (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and is made runnable when the socket is ready, so thousands of connections need only a few threads.
- Blocking syscalls and cgo calls: the M is stuck, so the P is handed off to another M (the `sysmon` background thread retakes it if the call takes too long). This is why heavy blocking file I/O or cgo can create many threads.

Since Go 1.14 preemption is **asynchronous**: sysmon signals a goroutine that has run for about 10ms, so tight loops can no longer starve others or stall GC. `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` prints scheduler state every second, and `go tool trace` visualises it.
takeaways: G = goroutine, M = OS thread, P = execution slot; GOMAXPROCS Ps
Idle Ps steal work; network I/O parks on the netpoller, not a thread
Blocking syscalls/cgo pin an M; preemption is asynchronous since 1.14
pitfalls: Setting GOMAXPROCS far above the container's CPU quota on old Go versions, causing throttling and latency spikes.

quiz.q: A goroutine blocks reading from a TCP socket. What happens to its OS thread (M)?
options: The thread blocks until data arrives
The goroutine is parked on the netpoller and the thread runs other goroutines
The runtime spins the thread until data is ready
quiz.explain: Network I/O is non-blocking under the hood; the G parks and the M continues with other work.

quiz.q: What does GOMAXPROCS limit?
options: The number of OS threads the process may create
How many goroutines can execute Go code at the same time
The size of each goroutine's stack
quiz.explain: It sets the number of Ps; threads blocked in syscalls don't hold a P, so the thread count can exceed it.

concepts.name: The Go memory model
concepts.summary: Happens-before, what synchronisation guarantees visibility, and why racy programs have no reliable meaning.
concepts.why: Correct lock-free and concurrent code depends on exactly which operations order memory between goroutines.
concepts.body:
The Go **memory model** answers one question: when is a goroutine guaranteed to see a write made by another? Without synchronisation, never — compilers and CPUs reorder and cache memory operations freely, as long as a single goroutine can't tell.

Guarantees come from **happens-before** edges created by synchronising operations:

- `go f()` happens before `f` starts.
- A send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes; closing a channel happens before a receive that returns because it's closed.
- For an unbuffered channel, a receive happens before the matching send completes. Generally, the k-th receive on a channel with capacity C happens before the (k+C)-th send completes — which is why a buffered channel works as a semaphore.
- `mu.Unlock()` happens before the next `mu.Lock()` returns. `once.Do(f)`: f's completion happens before any `Do` returns. `wg.Done` happens before the `Wait` it unblocks.
- `sync/atomic` operations are **sequentially consistent**: if an atomic load observes an atomic store, the store happens before the load.

Happens-before is transitive, so writes before a send are visible after the receive.

Since the 2022 revision (Go 1.19), Go promises **DRF-SC**: a program without data races behaves as if goroutines were interleaved on one core. With a race, guarantees mostly evaporate. Single-word races only expose some value that was written, but races on strings, slices, interfaces or maps can tear multi-word values and corrupt memory.
